content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Setting Up Your Development Environment

Install and configure the node and CLI, prepare the network files, and begin synchronization to a testnet.

16:9 HD Classroom

This chapter shows how the cardano-node maintains a local blockchain and how the cardano-cli sends commands to that node. You will learn how to place binaries, prepare genesis.json, topology.json and config.json, start a node with a socket path, and check sync progress with the CLI.

Why it matters: without a synced node you cannot construct valid transactions, query on-chain state reliably, or test integrations. A local node gives you an authoritative, programmable view of the blockchain for development and testing.

Explore Key Topics
Node & CLI
Why both are essential for querying and transacting.
Config Files
genesis.json, topology.json and config.json define network behavior.
Syncing & Verify
Monitor sync progress and confirm with cardano-cli query tip.
Visual Concept — Local Node Topology
cardano-node

Maintains and validates the blockchain. Stores the database and opens a Unix socket for CLI communication.

Database: db/ • Socket: node.socket • Runs: daemon process
cardano-cli

Command-line tool that constructs transactions, queries tips, and manages addresses by talking to the node over the socket path.

Usage: cardano-cli query tip --testnet-magic <magic>
Key Takeaway

Run a local node and use the CLI to interact with a synced, authoritative blockchain state before building wallets or contracts.

Coming up

Next we'll set learning objectives, then step through installation, configuration, running, verifying, and troubleshooting in hands-on detail.

First, you will identify the essential components of a development environment: a running cardano-node and the cardano-cli that talks to it. Second, you'll go through an installation and configuration workflow so you can place binaries in your PATH, prepare a node directory, and set the socket path. Third, we'll walk you through synchronizing to a testnet and verifying sync progress with a cardano-cli query, so you can be confident your node reflects the current chain. Finally, you'll learn how to recognize and fix common setup issues, such as network magic mismatches, insufficient disk space, and unstable peer connections. Each objective includes a short mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember, and a verified competency milestone that describes how you'll demonstrate the skill. By the end you'll be ready to start a node, watch it reach full sync, and run CLI queries to confirm success.

screens.title: cardano-node and cardano-cli — Roles and relationship
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the two core components you'll depend on. The cardano-node is the full node software that connects to the Cardano network, downloads blocks, validates them, and stores the blockchain history in a local database. Think of it as an authoritative mirror of the network running on your machine. The node also opens a Unix domain socket file that serves as the local channel for tools. The cardano-cli is a command-line program that constructs commands for the node — querying the tip, building transactions, and managing keys or addresses. The CLI does not maintain a copy of the chain; instead, it relies on the node's socket to submit requests and receive the node's view of the chain. A concrete example: when you run cardano-cli query tip with the correct testnet magic and socket path set, the CLI asks the node for the current tip and reports syncProgress. A common misconception is to think the CLI can operate without a node: it cannot. Without a running node and its socket, many CLI commands will fail to connect. The core insight is simple: the node maintains state and the CLI is the user's control panel for that state. Which operation will you try first to see this relationship in action?

keyIdea.title: Node stores state; CLI controls it
keyIdea.text: cardano-node holds the blockchain and exposes a socket; cardano-cli issues commands through that socket to query or construct transactions.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Roles & Relationship

cardano-node

Runs continuously, connects to peers, downloads and validates every block, and stores the database. It creates a socket file that other tools use to communicate.

• Persistent database for blocks and chain state.
• Exposes node.socket for local IPC.
• Must be running for CLI operations that query or submit transactions.

cardano-cli

A command-line interface for asking the node for data and constructing actions like transactions, queries, and address management. The CLI requires the node's socket path and the correct network magic.

• Sends requests over the socket to the running node.
• Builds raw transactions that the node can submit.
• Does not maintain chain data itself.
Example

Run cardano-cli query tip after starting a node to see syncProgress and the current block number returned by the node.

Common Mistake

Trying to use CLI commands without a running node or without setting the CARDANO_NODE_SOCKET_PATH leads to connection errors.

Key Takeaway

The node is the source of truth; the CLI is the tool that controls and queries it. Both are required for development.

screens.title: Installing cardano-node and cardano-cli
screens.narratorSegment: Installation starts with a deliberate choice: use pre-compiled binaries for speed and simplicity, or build from source when you need a custom build or the latest commit. For beginners, pre-compiled binaries reduce friction and are the recommended path. The steps are straightforward: download the cardano-node and cardano-cli binaries that match the network release you plan to use; make the binaries executable; and place them in a directory included in your PATH, such as /usr/local/bin. A concrete example: after downloading, you run chmod +x on each binary and then mv them into your bin directory so you can run cardano-node --version from any terminal. Common pitfalls include using binaries that are incompatible with your chosen config files or forgetting to export or persist PATH changes so the terminal cannot find the commands. If you prefer building from source, you'll need a Haskell toolchain and the node's repository; that path takes longer but gives you build-time control. Start by confirming the version parity between binaries and configuration files; a mismatch can cause obscure runtime errors. Which install path will you choose for your environment?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Install

Installation Steps

1. Choose binary or source
Binaries: faster. Build from source: more control and up-to-date commits.
2. Make executable & place in PATH
chmod +x cardano-node; mv cardano-node /usr/local/bin or add your bin to PATH.
3. Confirm versions
Run cardano-node --version and cardano-cli --version to ensure binaries are callable.

Quick Terminal Example

chmod +x cardano-node
chmod +x cardano-cli
mv cardano-node cardano-cli /usr/local/bin
cardano-node --version
cardano-cli --version
Misconception

Installing binaries alone is not enough — ensure the binaries match the network configuration files you will use when running the node.

Key Takeaway

Get binaries into your PATH and confirm their versions. Mismatched versions often cause runtime errors.

screens.title: Configuration files explained
screens.narratorSegment: Configuration files are the instructions a node uses to join and behave on a network. genesis. json defines the initial parameters of the network and the chain's starting point. topology. json lists peer nodes and how your node finds peers to download blocks from; it directly affects connectivity and how the node finds healthy peers. config. json contains operational settings such as slot length, protocol parameters and file paths the node relies on. A concrete example is using preview testnet configuration files: those three files are provided for that network and must match the network magic the node and CLI expect. A common misconception is that you can freely mix files from different networks; this leads to mismatched network behavior and connection errors because the genesis and config semantics differ. When preparing your node directory, place these files in the same folder you'll reference when running cardano-node run. If you update topology. json to point to healthy peers you can improve sync speed; conversely an empty or stale topology. json can slow or stall synchronization. Which config file will you inspect first when troubleshooting connectivity?

keyIdea.title: Configs determine network identity and peers
keyIdea.text: genesis.json sets chain parameters, topology.json lists peers for connectivity, and config.json controls node runtime behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Config Files
genesis.json

Defines the network's initial state and parameters. It identifies the correct chain history for the node to validate.

Must match the intended network.
topology.json

Lists peers the node will attempt to connect to. Healthy peers speed up synchronization; stale peers can stall it.

Update to include reachable, healthy peers for better sync.
config.json

Contains runtime parameters like slot length and logging. It controls operational behavior and protocol details.

Use the config provided for the same network as the genesis file.
Practical Example

Place all three files into your node directory (for example ~/cardano-dev/preview-node) and reference them when running cardano-node. Mismatched files are the usual cause of network identity errors.

Common Mistake

Mixing files from different networks causes network magic mismatches and connection failures.

Pro Tip

Keep a separate directory per network (preview, preprod, mainnet) to avoid accidental file mixing.

screens.title: Directory layout, socket path, and PATH setup
screens.narratorSegment: A tidy directory layout and a correctly set socket path make CLI interactions predictable. A recommended layout for a preview node is a directory such as ~/cardano-dev/preview-node containing the topology. json, config. json, genesis. json, a db directory, and the node. socket file created at runtime. Binaries can live in /usr/local/bin or a user bin folder added to PATH. The socket file is how cardano-cli and other tools communicate with the running node; ensure the CARDANO_NODE_SOCKET_PATH environment variable points to the node. socket location before running CLI commands. A practical example: set export CARDANO_NODE_SOCKET_PATH=~/cardano-dev/preview-node/node. socket in your shell, then run cardano-cli query tip --testnet-magic 2 to query the node. Common mistakes include forgetting to export the socket path or starting the CLI in a different shell session without the environment set. If the CLI reports it cannot find the socket, check the node process for the socket path and ensure permissions allow access. Good organization reduces friction when you run and stop the node repeatedly during development. Directory layout, socket path, and PATH setup means set cardano_node_socket_path to the node.socket file and keep a clear directory structure to avoid connection and permission issues.. In practical terms, organize binaries, configs and the node database for reliable operation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Directory & Socket

Recommended layout

Organize one folder per network to avoid mixing files. Keep binaries in a PATH-visible folder and the node data under a db subfolder.
~/cardano-dev/preview-node/
  ├─ config.json
  ├─ genesis.json
  ├─ topology.json
  ├─ node.socket  (created when node runs)
  └─ db/
Environment

Set CARDANO_NODE_SOCKET_PATH to the node.socket path before running CLI commands in a new terminal session.

Quick shell example

export CARDANO_NODE_SOCKET_PATH=~/cardano-dev/preview-node/node.socket
cardano-cli query tip --testnet-magic 2
# Expected: syncProgress: 100.00 when fully synced
Common Mistake

Starting CLI in a shell without the environment variable set leads to socket-not-found errors even when the node is running.

Key Takeaway

A consistent directory and an exported socket path make CLI commands reliable across terminal sessions.

screens.title: Start the node — command breakdown
screens.narratorSegment: When you start a node, each parameter you pass controls a critical part of its operation. The canonical command includes flags for topology, database path, socket path, host address, port, and config. For example: cardano-node run --topology ~/cardano-node-preview/topology. json --database-path ~/cardano-node-preview/db --socket-path ~/cardano-node-preview/node. socket --host-addr 127.0.0.1 --port 3001 --config ~/cardano-node-preview/config. json. In this command, topology. json tells the node which peers to contact; database-path is where it stores the blockchain data; socket-path is the IPC file other tools use; host-addr and port define the local listening address for peer connections; and config. json contains runtime and protocol settings. A practical tip: ensure the socket-path is inside the node directory and that the directory has enough space for the database. A frequent misconception is to omit the database-path or socket-path and rely on defaults; explicit paths reduce confusion when running multiple nodes. After you run this command, monitor the terminal output for block numbers and sync percentage. How would you confirm the node created the socket file and started accepting peers? Start the node — command breakdown means provide explicit topology, database, socket and config paths when starting the node so you can reproduce and troubleshoot runs.. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Start Command

Command

cardano-node run \
  --topology ~/cardano-node-preview/topology.json \
  --database-path ~/cardano-node-preview/db \
  --socket-path ~/cardano-node-preview/node.socket \
  --host-addr 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 3001 \
  --config ~/cardano-node-preview/config.json
This explicit command ensures the node uses the intended config and stores its database and socket where you expect them.

Parameter meanings

  • --topology: peer list used for initial connectivity.
  • --database-path: where blocks are written and validated.
  • --socket-path: IPC file other tools use to talk to the node.
  • --config: runtime and protocol settings that shape node behavior.
Misconception

Defaults may vary across environments; prefer explicit paths when running nodes for development to avoid accidental overlaps.

Check

Confirm node.socket appears in the given path and that the terminal shows peers and syncing progress after start.

screens.title: Synchronization (Syncing) explained
screens.narratorSegment: Synchronization is the process by which your node downloads, verifies, and applies every historical block so its local state matches the network. For a testnet like preview, syncing usually takes less time than mainnet, but it can still range from hours to days depending on network peers, disk speed, and internet bandwidth. The node requests blocks from peers listed in topology. json, validates signatures and block headers, and stores the data under the database path. Key resource considerations include disk capacity — mainnet requires hundreds of gigabytes while testnets need much less — and stable connectivity. As a concrete example, if your topology. json points to healthy peers and your disk is fast, you may see steady progress displayed as block numbers and a sync percentage in the node's terminal. A common misconception is that progress will always be linear; in practice it can stall or jump depending on peer availability and local IO. If syncing stalls, check disk space, peer entries in topology. json, and node logs for errors. The core idea is that full synchronization is mandatory for authoritative local queries and transaction submission.

keyIdea.title: Syncing reconstructs chain locally
keyIdea.text: Syncing downloads and validates all historical blocks to give your node an authoritative, local copy of the blockchain.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Synchronization

Sync timeline

Connect to peers
Node contacts peers listed in topology.json to start fetching blocks.
Download & validate
Blocks are downloaded, signatures and headers are validated, and entries are written to the database.
Catch up to tip
The node reaches the latest block and syncProgress becomes 100.00.

What affects duration

  • Available disk space and disk write speed.
  • Number and health of peers in topology.json.
  • Internet bandwidth and latency.
Common Mistake

Assuming mainnet and testnet sync times are similar. Mainnet has a much larger history and requires more disk and time.

Key Takeaway

Syncing is essential and may take significant time; plan for disk space, stable connectivity, and good peers.

screens.title: Verify sync using cardano-cli query tip

screens.title: Network Magic — identification and common mismatches
screens.narratorSegment: Network magic is the numeric identifier that distinguishes Cardano networks. Each network — mainnet, preview testnet, preprod testnet — has a unique network magic value that the node and CLI must agree on. If the CLI uses a different magic than the node, you'll get a network magic mismatch error. For example, preview uses magic 2 in our examples; using --testnet-magic 1 instead would cause the CLI to attempt to talk to a different network identity and fail. A concrete troubleshooting pattern: if you see a mismatch error, confirm the config. json and genesis. json you provided to the node are for the intended network and then pass the same magic to cardano-cli query commands. Another common mistake is copying a CLI command that uses the wrong magic flag; always verify the numeric value before running queries. The practical takeaway is to keep a small checklist: confirm config files' network identification, set the same --testnet-magic in the CLI, and verify the node's terminal output shows the network name you expect. This small alignment step prevents a frequent and otherwise confusing class of errors.

screens.title: Common setup issues and troubleshooting steps
screens.narratorSegment: During setup you'll encounter a few recurring issues. One is insufficient disk space: the node writes to a growing database and will fail or stop progressing if the disk fills. Diagnose this with standard OS tools and free space checks. A second issue is peer or topology problems: topology. json may contain unreachable peers or outdated entries, causing slow or stalled sync. Update topology. json with healthy peers or restart the node to find new peers. A third common problem is incorrect file paths or permissions for the socket, which blocks the CLI from connecting. Ensure the socket file exists, has the right permissions, and that CARDANO_NODE_SOCKET_PATH points to it. Another frequent issue is network magic mismatch between CLI and node. The troubleshooting pattern is: check node logs and terminal output for obvious errors, confirm config files match the chosen network, verify disk and memory availability, and restart the node if needed. A practical example: when sync stalls at 85%, check disk free space and topology. json peer health before changing configs. These straightforward checks resolve most setup failures. Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Troubleshooting

Common issues

• Disk space: node cannot write new blocks if disk is full.
• Peer connectivity: stale or unreachable peers slow sync.
• Socket path & permissions: CLI cannot connect without access to node.socket.
• Network magic mismatch: CLI and node disagree on network identity.

Troubleshooting steps

  1. Check disk free space and node logs for write errors.
  2. Verify topology.json peers and update to healthy peers if needed.
  3. Confirm CARDANO_NODE_SOCKET_PATH points to an existing node.socket and permissions allow access.
  4. Ensure the CLI --testnet-magic value matches the node's network magic.
  5. Restart the node to recover from transient network issues.
Example

If sync stalls at 85%, first free disk space, then check topology.json peer health, then review logs for specific error messages before making config changes.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: These three concepts are the foundation for running a local Cardano node. First, cardano-node is the core software that downloads, validates and stores the blockchain history; without it you cannot perform authoritative queries or submit transactions. Second, cardano-cli is the command-line tool that constructs queries and transactions for the running node; it must be pointed at the node's socket to operate. Third, synchronization is the process of downloading and validating all historical blocks until the node reaches the current tip; syncing can take hours or days depending on network and hardware. Keep these three ideas in mind as you install, configure and verify a node: the node provides state, the CLI is your interface, and syncing makes the node usable. A simple reflection: when you run a CLI query, ask yourself whether the node is running, whether the socket path is exported, and whether syncProgress is complete.

Welcome. In this chapter you will build a dependable local Cardano development environment by installing the cardano-node and cardano-cli, preparing network configuration files, and performing an initial synchronization to a preview testnet. We'll focus on the practical steps that let you run a node, verify its sync progress, and use the CLI to query the blockchain. You will also learn common pitfalls — for example, mismatched network magic or insufficient disk space — and simple troubleshooting moves you can apply right away. A concrete example you will follow is starting a preview testnet node using a directory like ~/cardano-dev/preview-node, placing binaries in your PATH, and running the provided cardano-node run command with topology, database, socket and config parameters. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to start a node, watch its sync progress until it reports one hundred percent, and run a cardano-cli query tip to confirm sync. Keep in mind a healthy local node is the foundation for wallet management, transaction construction, and all further development work. What small step will you try first: installing binaries or preparing config files?

In this lesson you will master the small but crucial set of skills needed to run a local Cardano node and use the command-line interface. First, you will identify the essential components of a development environment: a running cardano-node and the cardano-cli that talks to it. Second, you'll go through an installation and configuration workflow so you can place binaries in your PATH, prepare a node directory, and set the socket path. Third, we'll walk you through synchronizing to a testnet and verifying sync progress with a cardano-cli query, so you can be confident your node reflects the current chain. Finally, you'll learn how to recognize and fix common setup issues, such as network magic mismatches, insufficient disk space, and unstable peer connections. Each objective includes a short mnemonic or visual cue to help you remember, and a verified competency milestone that describes how you'll demonstrate the skill. By the end you'll be ready to start a node, watch it reach full sync, and run CLI queries to confirm success.

This second objectives slide connects the skills to measurable outcomes so you can verify readiness. For installation, you'll show the binaries are executable and can be invoked from the terminal without full paths. For configuration, you'll produce a node folder containing genesis. json, topology. json, and config. json aligned to the chosen network. For synchronization, your demonstration will be a cardano-cli query tip output that includes syncProgress equal to one hundred percent. For troubleshooting, you will explain how you resolved a simulated network magic mismatch by aligning the CLI flag to the node's configured magic or by replacing the wrong config file. Each measurable milestone closes the loop between knowledge and practice. Remember that these outcomes are short, repeatable checks you can perform immediately after setup: a visible node process, a socket file, and the cardano-cli tip response. These demonstrations reduce uncertainty and give you confidence to build wallets and transactions on top of a healthy node.

Let's define the two core components you'll depend on. The cardano-node is the full node software that connects to the Cardano network, downloads blocks, validates them, and stores the blockchain history in a local database. Think of it as an authoritative mirror of the network running on your machine. The node also opens a Unix domain socket file that serves as the local channel for tools. The cardano-cli is a command-line program that constructs commands for the node — querying the tip, building transactions, and managing keys or addresses. The CLI does not maintain a copy of the chain; instead, it relies on the node's socket to submit requests and receive the node's view of the chain. A concrete example: when you run cardano-cli query tip with the correct testnet magic and socket path set, the CLI asks the node for the current tip and reports syncProgress. A common misconception is to think the CLI can operate without a node: it cannot. Without a running node and its socket, many CLI commands will fail to connect. The core insight is simple: the node maintains state and the CLI is the user's control panel for that state. Which operation will you try first to see this relationship in action?

Installation starts with a deliberate choice: use pre-compiled binaries for speed and simplicity, or build from source when you need a custom build or the latest commit. For beginners, pre-compiled binaries reduce friction and are the recommended path. The steps are straightforward: download the cardano-node and cardano-cli binaries that match the network release you plan to use; make the binaries executable; and place them in a directory included in your PATH, such as /usr/local/bin. A concrete example: after downloading, you run chmod +x on each binary and then mv them into your bin directory so you can run cardano-node --version from any terminal. Common pitfalls include using binaries that are incompatible with your chosen config files or forgetting to export or persist PATH changes so the terminal cannot find the commands. If you prefer building from source, you'll need a Haskell toolchain and the node's repository; that path takes longer but gives you build-time control. Start by confirming the version parity between binaries and configuration files; a mismatch can cause obscure runtime errors. Which install path will you choose for your environment?

Configuration files are the instructions a node uses to join and behave on a network. genesis. json defines the initial parameters of the network and the chain's starting point. topology. json lists peer nodes and how your node finds peers to download blocks from; it directly affects connectivity and how the node finds healthy peers. config. json contains operational settings such as slot length, protocol parameters and file paths the node relies on. A concrete example is using preview testnet configuration files: those three files are provided for that network and must match the network magic the node and CLI expect. A common misconception is that you can freely mix files from different networks; this leads to mismatched network behavior and connection errors because the genesis and config semantics differ. When preparing your node directory, place these files in the same folder you'll reference when running cardano-node run. If you update topology. json to point to healthy peers you can improve sync speed; conversely an empty or stale topology. json can slow or stall synchronization. Which config file will you inspect first when troubleshooting connectivity?

A tidy directory layout and a correctly set socket path make CLI interactions predictable. A recommended layout for a preview node is a directory such as ~/cardano-dev/preview-node containing the topology. json, config. json, genesis. json, a db directory, and the node. socket file created at runtime. Binaries can live in /usr/local/bin or a user bin folder added to PATH. The socket file is how cardano-cli and other tools communicate with the running node; ensure the CARDANO_NODE_SOCKET_PATH environment variable points to the node. socket location before running CLI commands. A practical example: set export CARDANO_NODE_SOCKET_PATH=~/cardano-dev/preview-node/node. socket in your shell, then run cardano-cli query tip --testnet-magic 2 to query the node. These three concepts are the foundation for running a local Cardano node. First, cardano-node is the core software that downloads, validates and stores the blockchain history; without it you cannot perform authoritative queries or submit transactions. Second, cardano-cli is the command-line tool that constructs queries and transactions for the running node; it must be pointed at the node's socket to operate. Third, synchronization is the process of downloading and validating all historical blocks until the node reaches the current tip; syncing can take hours or days depending on network and hardware. Keep these three ideas in mind as you install, configure and verify a node: the node provides state, the CLI is your interface, and syncing makes the node usable. A simple reflection: when you run a CLI query, ask yourself whether the node is running, whether the socket path is exported, and whether syncProgress is complete.

These additional concepts help you run a reliable, secure node. Network magic distinguishes networks and must match between the node and CLI. Configuration files — genesis. json, topology. json and config. json — define the network identity, peer list, and runtime parameters and must be kept consistent. The socket path is the IPC file that cardano-cli uses to communicate with the node, and the CARDANO_NODE_SOCKET_PATH environment variable must point to it. Finally, practice safety by not exposing the node's A P I port publicly without proper firewall rules; for local development, keep the node bound to localhost. A short reflection: before you run any CLI command that depends on the current chain, ensure the socket, the testnet magic and the config files are aligned.
